examples.title: AND Gate
examples.summary: The simplest product term: the output is high only when both inputs are high.
examples.aim: Implement a two-input AND gate with a continuous assignment and verify all four input combinations.
examples.operation: The continuous assignment y = a & b is always active. Whenever a or b changes, the simulator evaluates the bitwise AND and drives y with the result. For single-bit signals, bitwise AND and logical AND agree, but the bitwise operator is the one that describes hardware.

statements.code: module and_gate (input wire a, input wire b, output wire y);
statements.text: Declares the module and its three single-bit ports. The design has no storage.
Continuously drives y from the AND of a and b. This is dataflow modelling.

observations: Only the 11 row produces a 1; the other three rows produce 0.
The output changes as soon as either input changes because the assignment is continuous.
The testbench checks all four rows and reports 4/4 matches.
mistakes: Using && instead of &: && is a logical operator that returns a one-bit result and is not the usual gate description.
Declaring y as a reg in a design that only uses assign; a continuous assignment drives a net.
Connecting the testbench ports in the wrong order instead of using named connections.
examples.revision: AND is the product term: Y = A · B. It is 1 only for A = 1 and B = 1.

examples.title: OR Gate
examples.summary: The sum term: the output is low only when every input is low.
examples.aim: Implement a two-input OR gate with a continuous assignment and verify all four input combinations.
examples.operation: The assignment y = a | b drives y high whenever at least one input is high. The only zero row is 00. Like the AND example, this is pure combinational logic with no clock and no stored state.

statements.code: module or_gate (input wire a, input wire b, output wire y);
statements.text: The module boundary names the inputs and the output.
The bitwise OR operator describes the gate. It is not the logical || operator.

observations: Three rows produce 1 and only 00 produces 0.
OR is not the same as XOR: 11 still produces 1 for OR.
The testbench reports 4/4 rows match.
mistakes: Using || instead of | and expecting a multi-bit gate.
Confusing OR with XOR when the inputs are both high.
Leaving an output undriven by forgetting the assign statement.
examples.revision: OR is the sum term: Y = A + B. It is 0 only when A = 0 and B = 0.

examples.title: XOR Gate
examples.summary: The difference detector: the output is high when the two inputs disagree.
examples.aim: Implement a two-input XOR gate and verify its four-row truth table.
examples.operation: The assignment y = a ^ b produces 1 when exactly one input is high. XOR is also the one-bit parity function, which is why it appears inside adders and subtractors. It is combinational and has no memory.

statements.code: module xor_gate (input wire a, input wire b, output wire y);
statements.text: A small module with two inputs and one output.
The ^ operator is bitwise XOR. For 1-bit operands it is the gate function.

observations: The 01 and 10 rows produce 1; the equal rows 00 and 11 produce 0.
XOR is not OR: the 11 row is 0, not 1.
The testbench reports 4/4 rows match.
mistakes: Calling XOR inclusive OR and expecting 11 to be 1.
Using ^~ when XNOR is intended.
Forgetting that XOR is a parity function when it is extended to wider vectors.
examples.revision: XOR is inequality: Y = A ⊕ B. It is 1 when the inputs differ and 0 when they match.

examples.title: Half Adder
examples.summary: Adds two one-bit inputs and produces a sum and a carry.
examples.aim: Build a half adder from XOR and AND, then compare every row with the decimal sum A + B.
examples.operation: The sum bit is A XOR B because 1 + 1 produces 0 in the current column and a carry. The carry bit is A AND B because a carry is generated only when both inputs are 1. There is no carry input, so this circuit cannot be chained directly without extra logic.

statements.text: The current-column result of adding two bits.
The carry generated when both inputs are high.

observations: 1 + 1 gives sum 0 and carry 1, which is decimal 2 when the carry is included.
The decimal column in the transcript is computed with integers, so it shows 2 rather than a wrapped one-bit value.
The testbench reports 4/4 rows match.
mistakes: Forgetting the carry output and treating the circuit as a one-bit adder only.
Computing the decimal sum with one-bit arithmetic in the testbench, which hides the carry.
Trying to chain half adders without an extra OR gate for the incoming carry.
examples.revision: Half adder: S = A ⊕ B, C = A · B. It adds two bits but has no carry input.

examples.title: Full Adder
examples.summary: Adds three one-bit inputs, including a carry-in, and produces sum and carry-out.
examples.aim: Implement a full adder from Boolean equations and verify all eight input combinations.
examples.operation: The sum is the parity of A, B and Cin, so it is high for an odd number of ones. The carry is the majority function: it is high when at least two of the three inputs are high. The expression (A · B) + (Cin · (A ⊕ B)) is a compact majority form.

statements.text: Three-input parity gives the sum bit.
Carry is generated by A and B, or propagated by Cin through exactly one of them.

observations: Rows with an odd number of ones have sum 1; rows with two or three ones have carry 1.
The decimal column shows 3 for 1 + 1 + 1, not a wrapped one-bit value.
The testbench reports 8/8 rows match.
mistakes: Using OR instead of XOR for the sum, which fails when all three inputs are high.
Forgetting the carry-in term in the carry expression.
Reversing the carry-out and sum connections in a larger adder.
examples.revision: Full adder: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = A·B + Cin·(A ⊕ B). It is the building block of a ripple-carry adder.

examples.title: Half Subtractor
examples.summary: Subtracts B from A and reports the difference and the borrow.
examples.aim: Implement a half subtractor and verify all four input combinations, including the negative decimal case.
examples.operation: The difference is A XOR B, the same parity function used by the half adder. The borrow is high only for 0 − 1, which is (~A) AND B. Subtraction is not symmetric: A − B and B − A produce different borrows.

statements.text: The difference bit for two one-bit operands.
A borrow is needed only when A is 0 and B is 1.

observations: The 0 − 1 row gives difference 1 and borrow 1, which represents −1 in two's-complement style arithmetic.
The decimal column shows −1 rather than the unsigned wrap value 1.
The testbench reports 4/4 rows match.
mistakes: Using A AND ~B for the borrow, which is the borrow for B − A.
Forgetting that the decimal result can be negative.
Assuming a half subtractor can accept a borrow-in.
examples.revision: Half subtractor: D = A ⊕ B, Bout = ~A · B. It subtracts two bits and has no borrow input.

examples.title: Full Subtractor
examples.summary: Subtracts B and a borrow-in from A, producing difference and borrow-out.
examples.aim: Implement a full subtractor and verify all eight input combinations.
examples.operation: The difference is the parity of A, B and Bin. The borrow-out is high when A is 0 and B is 1, or when the difference term is 0 and Bin is 1. The decimal column uses signed integers in the testbench so negative results are visible.

statements.text: Three-input parity gives the difference bit.
Borrow is generated directly, or propagated through the current difference.

observations: The 0 − 1 − 1 row produces difference 0 and borrow 1, representing −2.
The borrow-out depends on Bin as well as A and B.
The testbench reports 8/8 rows match.
mistakes: Dropping the Bin term from the borrow expression.
Treating the borrow as A < B only and ignoring the incoming borrow.
Printing the decimal result with one-bit arithmetic and losing the sign.
examples.revision: Full subtractor: D = A ⊕ B ⊕ Bin, Bout = ~A·B + ~(A ⊕ B)·Bin. It is the subtractor counterpart of the full adder.

examples.title: 4-Bit Ripple-Carry Adder
examples.summary: Chains four full adders to add two four-bit numbers with a carry-in.
examples.aim: Build a four-bit ripple-carry adder from four full-adder instances and sweep all 512 input combinations.
examples.operation: Each full adder handles one bit position. The carry from bit 0 feeds bit 1, and so on. The final carry is the unsigned carry-out. Signed overflow is not the same signal: it is the XOR of the carry into and out of the most significant bit, which the design exposes as overflow.

statements.text: The first stage adds the least significant bits and the incoming carry.
The last carry becomes the unsigned carry-out.
Signed overflow is the mismatch between the carry entering and leaving the sign bit.

observations: The testbench checks all 512 combinations of A, B and Cin.
8 + 8 produces sum 0000, carry-out 1 and overflow 1: unsigned 16 is negative in four-bit signed arithmetic.
15 + 15 + 1 produces sum 1111 and carry-out 1, but no signed overflow.
The transcript prints five representative rows and the 512/512 summary.
mistakes: Treating carry-out as signed overflow; they answer different questions.
Reversing the carry chain so bit 0 receives the final carry.
Using a 4-bit expression for the expected sum and losing the fifth bit.
examples.revision: A ripple-carry adder chains full adders. Sum is modulo 16 for four bits; carry-out is unsigned overflow, while signed overflow is carry[2] XOR carry[3].

examples.title: 4:1 Multiplexer
examples.summary: Routes one of four data inputs to a single output under a two-bit select.
examples.aim: Implement a 4:1 multiplexer with a behavioural case statement and verify all 64 select/data combinations.
examples.operation: The select input chooses which data bit reaches y. Only one branch of the case statement is active at a time. A default branch keeps the output defined even if the select value were unknown or out of range, which also helps avoid an accidental latch.

statements.text: A combinational procedural block: it re-evaluates whenever a read signal changes.
Selects exactly one data input for each select value.
Keeps the output defined and makes the intent explicit.

observations: With d = 1010, select 00 gives 0, 01 gives 1, 10 gives 0 and 11 gives 1.
All 64 combinations of four data bits and four select values are checked.
The output is purely combinational; there is no clock.
mistakes: Forgetting the default branch and inferring a latch in some tools.
Swapping the select bit order so S1 and S0 are reversed.
Using blocking assignments in a clocked block when combinational behaviour is intended.
examples.revision: A 4:1 multiplexer is a selector: Y = D[S], where S is the two-bit select value. It is the routing element of a datapath.

examples.title: 1:4 Demultiplexer
examples.summary: Sends one data input to exactly one of four outputs.
examples.aim: Implement a 1:4 demultiplexer and verify all eight data/select combinations.
examples.operation: The output vector is cleared to 0000 first, then the selected bit is driven with din. This one-hot style means exactly one output can be high, and all unselected outputs stay low. The select input is the destination address.

statements.text: Clears every output before selecting one destination.
Routes din to the output named by sel.

observations: When din = 0, every output is 0 regardless of select.
When din = 1, exactly one output is 1 and the other three are 0.
The testbench checks all eight combinations.
mistakes: Forgetting to clear the other outputs, so old values remain high.
Driving the same output from two branches.
Confusing a demultiplexer with a decoder: a demux routes data, while a decoder asserts a selected line.
examples.revision: A 1:4 demultiplexer is the reverse of a multiplexer: one input is routed to one of four outputs. The unselected outputs must be driven low.

examples.title: 2-to-4 Decoder with Enable
examples.summary: Converts a two-bit address into one active output line, with an enable input.
examples.aim: Implement a 2-to-4 decoder with an active-high enable and verify all eight enable/address combinations.
examples.operation: When enable is low, all four outputs are forced low. When enable is high, exactly one output is high according to the address. This is a one-hot decoder, not a data router: there is no data input to pass through.

statements.text: The enable gates the whole decoder.
Maps each address to one active output.

observations: With enable = 0, every address produces 0000.
With enable = 1, address 00 produces 0001, 01 produces 0010, 10 produces 0100 and 11 produces 1000.
The testbench checks all eight combinations.
mistakes: Treating enable as active-low without inverting it.
Using a decoder as a demultiplexer and expecting a data input.
Forgetting the default branch and leaving outputs undefined.
examples.revision: A 2-to-4 decoder asserts one of four lines for each address. The enable input can disable every output at once.

examples.title: 4-to-2 Priority Encoder
examples.summary: Reports the highest-numbered active request as a two-bit code.
examples.aim: Implement a four-input priority encoder with a valid output and verify all 16 request patterns.
examples.operation: The if/else-if chain checks req[3] first, then req[2], req[1] and req[0]. The first high request wins. If no request is high, code is 00 and valid is 0; valid distinguishes the no-request case from a genuine request on req[0].

statements.text: The default is valid; the no-request branch clears it.
The order of the branches implements priority.
Handles the no-request case explicitly.

observations: Request 0000 gives code 00 and valid 0.
Request 0001 gives code 00 and valid 1, so valid is essential.
Request 1111 gives code 11 because req[3] has the highest priority.
The testbench checks all 16 patterns.
mistakes: Reversing the priority order and checking req[0] first.
Forgetting the valid output and making 0000 indistinguishable from 0001.
Using casex instead of casez without understanding the difference between don't-care and unknown values.
examples.revision: A priority encoder reports the most significant active request. The valid bit separates a real request on line 0 from no request at all.

examples.title: D Flip-Flop with Enable and Reset
examples.summary: Stores one bit on a rising clock edge, with an enable and an asynchronous reset.
examples.aim: Implement a positive-edge D flip-flop and verify reset, hold, load and no-edge behaviour.
examples.operation: The always block triggers on a rising clock edge or a rising reset edge. Reset clears q immediately, without waiting for a clock. When reset is low and enable is high, the next rising edge copies d into q. When enable is low, the stored value holds. qbar is the continuous complement of q. The testbench checks both q and qbar.

statements.text: A positive-edge clock with an asynchronous active-high reset.

statements.code: if (rst) q <= 1'b0; else if (en) q <= d;
statements.text: Reset has priority; enable gates the load.
The complement output follows q continuously.

observations: Changing d while the clock is steady does not change q.
Enable low holds the old value across a rising edge.
Reset high clears q immediately, even without a clock edge.
The testbench reports 8/8 state checks match.
mistakes: Using blocking assignments in a clocked block and creating a race.
Treating enable as a clock and expecting a level-sensitive latch.
Assuming reset waits for the next clock edge when it is asynchronous.
Forgetting that qbar must be a wire driven by a continuous assignment.
examples.revision: A D flip-flop samples D on the active clock edge. Enable decides whether the edge loads; asynchronous reset overrides the clock and clears the state.

examples.title: 4-Bit Behavioural ALU
examples.summary: Selects AND, OR, addition or subtraction from a two-bit operation code.
examples.aim: Implement a small combinational ALU with a behavioural case statement and verify all four operations on two data pairs.
examples.operation: The always @* block is combinational: every output depends only on the current inputs. The case statement selects one operation. Addition and subtraction are four-bit operations, so the result wraps modulo 16; the testbench expects that truncation. The same function could be written as a dataflow conditional expression, which is a useful comparison.

statements.text: Re-evaluates whenever a, b or op changes.
One branch for each operation code.
Keeps the output defined for unexpected codes.

observations: Operation 00 performs bitwise AND; 01 performs bitwise OR.
Operation 10 adds modulo 16; operation 11 subtracts modulo 16.
The testbench checks eight operation/data pairs and reports 8/8 matches.
mistakes: Forgetting the default branch and inferring a latch.
Expecting a carry or overflow output that this small ALU does not provide.
Mixing blocking and non-blocking assignments in a combinational block.
examples.revision: A behavioural ALU uses a case statement to select an operation. It is still combinational hardware: no clock, no stored state, and a defined output for every input.
